name: Kingdom of Sweden (medieval)
summary: The Swedish kingdom from its Christianisation to the eve of its great-power age; it ruled Finland, joined the Kalmar Union (1397–1523) and broke away under Gustav Vasa.

location.value: Svealand and Götaland, first ruled together by Olof Skötkonung, with Finland later part of the kingdom. The page does not name Lake Mälaren or medieval Gotland.

terrain.value: Forests of pine and spruce, thousands of lakes, mining hills in Bergslagen, a rocky coast and the island of Gotland.

climate.value: Cold winters with snow and ice, and short, mild summers; the north was colder still, limiting farming.

resources.value: Iron and copper (notably at Falun), timber, furs, fish, and farmland in the south and around Lake Mälaren.

disasters.value: The Black Death reached Sweden in 1350 and killed perhaps a third or more of the people, followed by later plague waves.

population.value: The Black Death killed a third of the population in 1349–1351 and numbers did not recover to pre-1348 levels until the early 19th century; the page gives no total for around 1500, so the earlier estimate of about 750,000 is not confirmed here.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Swedish settlers moved into coastal Finland from the 1100s–1200s, and German merchants and miners settled in Swedish towns.

economicBase.value: Sweden remained poor and underdeveloped, with barter the main means of exchange, and Gustav Vasa broke the Hanseatic League’s trade monopoly; the page does not mention medieval iron, copper or butter exports.

tradeRoutes.value: Baltic trade dominated by the Hanseatic League; Visby on Gotland and Stockholm traded with Lübeck and Novgorod.

wealth.value: Iron and copper from Bergslagen and Falun brought wealth to the crown, mine owners and German merchants.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver pennies (örtugar and marks) minted from the late 1100s; taxes paid in coins, goods and labour.

inequality.value: Free peasants were stronger than elsewhere.

governmentType.value: The monarchy became hereditary in 1544; the page does not describe the earlier elective system.

keyRulers.value: Birger Jarl led the Second Swedish Crusade, bringing Finland gradually into the kingdom; Magnus Ladulås reigned 1275–1290; the nobles made Gustav Vasa king on 6 June 1523.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Sweden (checked 13 Nov 2026); Swedish History Museum: Middle Ages (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Birger Jarl founded towns and introduced laws; Magnus Ladulås not covered)

succession.value: Kings were elected at the Stones of Mora; the Riksdag made the monarchy hereditary in the Vasa family in 1544.

institutions.value: A Council of the Realm of nobles and bishops, national law codes (about 1350), and the Riksdag, with peasants as an estate.

stability.value: Often unstable: rival kings, the Kalmar Union struggles, and the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520, when Christian II executed about 80 nobles.

eliteConflict.value: Swedish nobles and regents, such as the Sture family, struggled against the Danish kings of the Kalmar Union.

armyAndTech.value: Armed peasant levies, noble cavalry and castles; Gustav Vasa created a standing army and bought a navy from Lübeck (1522).

majorWars.value: Christian II’s massacre of Swedish nobles in 1520 renewed resistance, which ended with Gustav Vasa’s election as king in 1523; the Kalmar Union lasted from 17 June 1397 to 6 June 1523. The page does not name a “War of Liberation”.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Sweden (checked 13 Nov 2026); Swedish History Museum: Middle Ages (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Kalmar Union formed 1397 and unstable, with the Engelbrekt rising in the 1430s and the Stockholm bloodbath in 1520)

territoryChange.value: Brought Finland under Swedish rule in the 1100s–1200s; the Treaty of Nöteborg (1323) set a border with Novgorod; took Estonia (1561).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivalry with Denmark for Baltic power, wars with Novgorod and Russia, and dependence on the Hanseatic city of Lübeck.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Swedish miners were skilled in iron and copper working.

scienceEducation.value: Uppsala University (1477) was the first in Scandinavia; monasteries such as Vadstena kept libraries and schools.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Rough roads, rivers and lakes, sledges on winter ice, and coastal shipping across the Baltic.

religion.value: Gustav Vasa rejected Catholicism and led Sweden into the Reformation (a Riksdag met in 1527, though the page does not name Västerås); the Uppsala Synod of 1593 confirmed the Church of Sweden as Lutheran. The 1164 archbishopric is not mentioned.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Sweden (checked 13 Nov 2026); Swedish History Museum: Middle Ages; Britannica: Sweden, The early Vasa kings (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Christianity replaced Norse religion in the 11th century; Britannica: the Diet of Västerås (1527) let the crown take Church property, which held about 21% of the land against 6% for the crown, and Lutheranism became the state church)

languageWriting.value: Old Swedish written in runes and later the Latin alphabet; Latin for the Church; the first Swedish Bible printed in 1541.

artsArchitecture.value: Stone churches and Uppsala Cathedral, painted church ceilings by Albertus Pictor, and the medieval walls of Visby.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to king, faith and home province; resistance to Danish rule helped shape a Swedish identity.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: Denmark (which then held Scania), Norway, Novgorod and later Russia, the Teutonic Order and the Hanseatic towns.

ideasReligions.value: The Lutheran Reformation, brought by Olaus Petri and the king from the 1520s; earlier, St Bridget’s religious movement.

colonisation.value: Swedish rule and settlement spread into Finland through crusades in the 1100s–1200s; Finland remained part of the realm.

riseSignals.value: A unified Swedish state was established in the late 10th century; the Swedish Viking Age lasted roughly from the eighth to the 11th century.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Sweden (checked 13 Nov 2026); Swedish History Museum: Middle Ages (checked 14 Nov 2026) (the museum says Sweden began as several small kingdoms and chiefdoms and dates the Middle Ages to about 1050–1520; King Olof Skötkonung’s baptism is dated by coins to 995–1005)

peakPeriod.value: The early Vasa era: Gustav Vasa was crowned in 1523, took Church lands (21% of the farmland, approved at Västerås in 1527) and built what the page calls the first modern army in Europe. A navy is not mentioned.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: History of Sweden (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Sweden, The early Vasa kings (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Britannica: by Gustav Vasa’s death the crown held about 60% of Swedish land and the monarchy was hereditary from 1544)

declineSignals.value: No real decline: by the early 1600s Sweden was growing into a major Baltic power, the Swedish Empire.

outcome.value: Sweden joined the Kalmar Union in 1397 and left it in 1523, when Gustav Vasa was made king on 6 June 1523.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Sweden (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Sweden, The early Vasa kings (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Gustav Vasa elected 1523; Treaty of Malmö with Denmark 1524)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
